analysis.one_liner: Adds outpatient prescription drug coverage to Medicare, requiring manufacturers to pay rebates and disclose prices.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. David Pryor with one cosponsor in June 1994, never received a committee vote before Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a limited Medicare outpatient drug benefit — covering transplant anti-rejection drugs, dialysis drugs, and oral cancer chemotherapy — and required drug makers to sign rebate agreements paying Medicare at least a set share of their retail price, with room to negotiate larger rebates on expensive new drugs. It would have pushed prescribing toward cheaper generics, required pharmacists to review and counsel on prescriptions, published drug price information in the US and abroad, and required manufacturers to offer their discounts to all buyers on equal terms rather than reserving them for big purchasers. The Senate Finance Committee, to which it was referred, never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who need drugs the program currently excludes — transplant patients on immunosuppressants, dialysis patients needing erythropoietin, and cancer patients on oral chemotherapy — would gain coverage. Taxpayers and beneficiaries would benefit from mandatory manufacturer rebates, greater use of generics, and published price information that could hold down drug prices. Consumers generally would benefit from pharmacist counseling and drug-use review meant to catch dangerous prescriptions.

how_it_helps.text: Adds outpatient prescription drugs to Medicare for specific groups: transplant patients' immunosuppressants (with the covered window expanding from 12 to 36 months after transplant), erythropoietin for dialysis patients, and FDA-approved oral anticancer chemotherapy drugs [S2][S3].

Conditions Medicare payment on manufacturers signing rebate agreements — a basic rebate of 17 percent off the average manufacturer retail price for brand-name and single-source drugs, with the Secretary authorized to negotiate higher rebates for new drugs and to exclude from coverage drugs whose makers refuse to negotiate [S2][S3].

Requires a generic-only dispensing policy for drugs with three or more equivalent versions, and bars payment for brand-name versions of such drugs unless the physician writes 'brand medically necessary' on the prescription — in Medicare and Medicaid alike [S2][S3].

Requires a drug use review program in Medicare, paying pharmacists for reviewing prescriptions before filling them, counseling patients on use and side effects, and case-managing high-risk patients [S2][S3].

Creates a Pharmaceutical Marketplace Information Commission to publish US and international drug prices, investigate whether manufacturers offer discounts to all buyers on equal terms, and assess whether the prices of breakthrough drugs are reasonable; its findings would be public but not binding [S2][S3].

Requires manufacturers of brand-name and single-source drugs to offer every purchaser the same rebates, discounts, and free merchandise on equal terms — addressing the bill's finding that discounts offered to some large buyers were not extended to all, which raised retail prices for consumers [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the largest cost: mandatory quarterly rebates, inflation-based additional rebates, penalties up to $100,000 for false or withheld price information, and the end of selectively discounted deals. Health plans and pharmacies would take on compliance costs for drug-use review, formularies, and counseling. Patients who genuinely need brand-name drugs would face extra paperwork and possible prior authorization. The Medicare program would take on new spending for the drug coverage itself, offset in part by the rebates.

drawbacks.text: The generic-first rules could slow access for the minority of patients who genuinely need a brand-name drug: prescribers would have to write 'brand medically necessary' in their own handwriting with justification, and the Secretary could require prior authorization, subjecting those patients to approval delays [S3].

The Secretary could exclude a new drug from Medicare coverage entirely, or limit it to protocol uses, if unable to negotiate an acceptable rebate — a real risk of delaying access to brand-new therapies for Medicare patients [S3].

The bill imposes heavy reporting and compliance duties: quarterly price reporting with fines up to $10,000 per day for late filings, state-level formulary and pharmacy-committee mandates on health plans, and new payment systems for pharmacists — administrative costs that would land somewhere in the system [S3].
The price-review commission's findings would have no binding effect on manufacturers, so its main tool is public exposure rather than enforcement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients left out — transplant, dialysis, and oral-chemotherapy patients with no Medicare drug coverage — the benefit is direct and substantial, and the rebate and transparency provisions push prices down for everyone. The main costs are administrative complexity and friction for the small share of patients who need brand-name drugs, which the bill tries to soften with 24-hour prior-authorization responses and emergency 72-hour supplies. It is a narrowly targeted benefit rather than a universal drug benefit, and its price provisions rely on negotiation and publicity rather than hard price caps, so its squeeze on drug prices would depend heavily on execution.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late June 1994 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never scheduled it for consideration before that Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Sen. David Pryor of Arkansas, joined by Sen. Harlan Sasser of Tennessee, introduced the bill on June 24, 1994 [S1][S4][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was taken: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote are recorded before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].
The bill arrived at the peak of the 1994 health care reform debate, which ended without major health legislation passing that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: no Medicare rebate mandate, no negotiated price reviews, and no equal-terms discount requirement took effect. Medicare beneficiaries without outpatient drug coverage for these conditions gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. David Pryor (D-AR)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill.

against.name: Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan (D-NY)
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never brought the bill to a markup during the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers (brand-name industry)
against.role: Industry group lobbying against Medicare drug price controls and rebate mandates
against.what_they_did: Opposed the 1994 wave of Medicare drug rebate and price-control legislation, including through the industry's campaign against the broader health reform effort that year.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats sponsored the bill and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows no roll calls that reveal how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill forces quarterly rebates of at least 17 percent of retail price on drugs sold to Medicare, allows negotiated higher rebates on new drugs with coverage exclusion as leverage, imposes fines for false or late price reporting, and requires discounts be offered to all buyers on equal terms. Its gains come from prices ordinary patients and taxpayers pay.

A generic-only dispensing policy for drugs with three or more equivalent versions, plus caps on brand-name dispensing in Medicaid, would route more prescriptions and sales to generic makers while lowering drug costs for beneficiaries.
The bill requires Medicare to pay pharmacists for prospective drug review, patient counseling, and pharmaceutical care services, creating a new paid role for them in the Medicare drug program.

industries.industry: Health plans and managed care insurers
industries.note: The bill is deliberately structured on managed-care principles and adds Medicare as a covered purchaser, but it also forces every plan covering drugs in Medicaid states to run pharmacy committees, formularies, and pharmacy care programs, with loss of federal payments for noncompliance.
